summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity on the initial removal of an Illinois child but vacated as to continuing to hold him after probable cause dissipated and as to the coerced safety plan, remanding those claims for further proceedings.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that the Juvenile Court Act's 48-hour window does not license continued custody once probable cause has dissipated.
key_cases.quote: Probable cause is determined on the basis of the facts and circumstances known to the defendants at the time of the conduct in issue

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a former foster child's section 1983 claims, holding that a child removed from his home on allegedly fabricated neglect allegations stated Fourth Amendment and substantive due process claims that survived the defendants' immunity defenses in part.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the constitutional ceiling on emergency protective custody in Illinois.
key_cases.quote: a seizure is reasonable if it is pursuant to a court order, if it is supported by probable cause, or if it is justified by exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that Illinois violated due process and equal protection by declaring the children of an unwed father dependent without any hearing on his fitness, and reversed the Illinois Supreme Court.
key_cases.relevance: Emergency custody cannot ripen into a change of custody without the hearing due process requires.
key_cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

key_cases.case_name: Siliven v. Indiana Department of Child Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for the caseworkers, holding that a removal made without a court order is reasonable only if supported by probable cause or exigent circumstances and that a physician's opinion of inflicted injury plus a prior abuse allegation supplied probable cause here.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the objective probable-cause framework for protective custody, judged on the facts known to the caseworker when the decision was made.
key_cases.quote: The pertinent inquiry, then, is whether defendants had probable cause to believe that C.S.'s physical health would be seriously endangered if he was not immediately removed from his father's custody.

search_keywords: Illinois Department of Children and Family Services

state_agency.name: Illinois Department of Children and Family Services

mandatory_reporters: Medical personnel — physicians, residents, interns, psychiatrists, surgeons, dentists, dental hygienists, chiropractic and podiatric physicians, physician assistants, emergency medical technicians, physical and occupational therapists, acupuncturists, registered/licensed practical/advanced practice nurses, genetic counselors, respiratory care practitioners, home health aides, certified nursing assistants — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(1)

Social services and mental health personnel — licensed counselors, social workers, psychologists, marriage and family therapists, field personnel of Healthcare and Family Services, Public Health, Human Services, Human Rights and DCFS, General Assistance supervisors/administrators, social services administrators, substance abuse treatment personnel — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(2)
Crisis intervention personnel — crisis line or hotline personnel, domestic violence program personnel — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(3)

Education personnel — school personnel (administrators, certified and non-certified employees), personnel of institutions of higher education, educational advocates, school board members (to the extent required by subsection (d)), truant officers — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(4)
Recreation or athletic program or facility personnel; athletic trainers — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(5)
Child care personnel — early intervention providers, nursery school and early care and education center directors and staff, foster parents, homemakers, child care workers — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(6)

Law enforcement personnel — law enforcement officers, Department of Juvenile Justice and Department of Corrections field personnel, probation officers, animal control officers and Department of Agriculture field investigators — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(7)
Funeral home directors and employees; coroners; medical examiners — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(8)
Any member of the clergy — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(9)
Medical, nursing, social work and counseling personnel of any office or clinic that provides abortions, abortion referrals, or contraceptives — 325 ILCS 5/4(a)(10)
reporting_details: Illinois is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals listed in 325 ILCS 5/4(a) must report, any other person may report voluntarily under 325 ILCS 5/4(f), and every report goes to the single statewide DCFS hotline required by 325 ILCS 5/7.6 (1-800-25-ABUSE / 1-800-252-2873).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours; immediately, regardless of the time of day or night, if the child's immediate safety or well-being is endangered or the family may flee (325 ILCS 5/7.4(b)(2))
60 days to determine "indicated" or "unfounded"; extendable in additional periods of up to 30 days for good cause (325 ILCS 5/7.12)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Report may be deemed "undetermined" where a complete investigation was not possible (325 ILCS 5/7.12)

timeline_requirements.deadline: 48 hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and court-designated holidays (705 ILCS 405/2-9(1))
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child taken into temporary protective custody
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The child must be released from temporary protective custody if not brought before a judicial officer within the 48 hours (705 ILCS 405/2-9(3))
